houses.key_references: Ballu III: 27-28; BCTH 1907: 272-273; Germain 1969: 130, fig. 18; Gsell AA f. 27, 255, 44; Inv. Mos. III: 109-111; Laghmouche 2024: Table 1, p. 224 (lists the NORTH house, not this one — negative citation); Lepelley 1981: 447-450
houses.notes: Christofle 1938 (pp. 355-356, section '1° FOUILLES DE LA COLLINE AU SUD DU CAPITOLE') reports 1933 excavations on the hill south of the Capitol that re-examine the Temple of Mercury initially signalled by Ballu in Sept années de découvertes (1911), p. 29. Christofle confirms the temple's existence but corrects the orientation: the building is clearly oriented N.-S., NOT E.-W. as Ballu had stated. The cella rested on three small barrel-vaulted rooms; an excellent E.-W. cross-wall is interpreted as part of the temple precinct enclosure. A larger platform of pebble-mortar concrete (cailloutis), 22 × 33 m, lay 10 m from the south wall of the Capitol courtyard on the axis of the cella, oriented N.W.-S.E.; a third monument c. 10 × 22 m, oriented N.-S., was identified some 10 m further away. A post-Roman cemetery — interpreted by Christofle as Berber or possibly Arab on the basis of W.-E. orientation, lack of grave goods in male burials, and bead necklaces of carnelian, painted glass, or coral plus two bronze bracelets in female burials — was installed across this hill. Note: this row's House Name says 'au Nord du Capitole' but its Mapping Notes and Location columns both say 'South of Capitol' — the pre-existing discrepancy is unresolved; the Christofle 1938 evidence pertains specifically to the hill SOUTH of the Capitol. [Source: Christofle 1938 (BIAA-Af-Alg-24): pp. 355-356]

LVIII; Christofle, Rapport 1927-1929 (publ. 1930): 58-62, plan p. 59; Courtois: 82; Germain 1969: 88-90, fig. 12; Gsell AA f. 27, 255, 56; Inv. Mos. III: 95-98; L'Architecture 1913: 99; Christofle 1930: 58-62; Laghmouche 2024: Table 1, p. 224 (chapter 219-227); Assassi & Mebarki 2021
houses.notes: Christofle 1938 (p. 359, section '3° FOUILLES AU NORD DU DECUMANUS MAXIMUS EN FACE LE CIMETIERE CHRETIEN ET LE LIEU DIT « ENTREPOT »') cites the Entrepôt as a topographical landmark when describing 1933 excavations on the north side of the Decumanus Maximus opposite the Christian cemetery. The 50 × 32 m excavation behind three lowered sidewalk kerbs (cart ruts still visible) revealed three contiguous private Roman houses: (A) an easternmost house with a portico supported by 6 square pilasters 0.50 m on a side (bases and lower piers in place); (B) a middle house with vestibule giving onto a paved courtyard around a 5 m-deep well (its upper part masonry, lower part dry-stone) — fragments of a fine bronze palm recovered from the well shaft; grooves 0.20 m wide in the surrounding paving once held vertical slabs forming the well-curb (margelle); (C) a westernmost house, the most damaged, immediately adjacent to the Lambèse Gate — interior divisions wholly lost. These three houses lie immediately north of/opposite the Entrepôt and would be the closest known elite domestic neighbours to it. [Source: Christofle 1938 (BIAA-Af-Alg-24): p. 359]
